questions.stem: In a coal-based thermal power plant, the correct sequence of energy transformations from fuel to electricity is:

options.option_text: Chemical → Thermal → Mechanical → Electrical energy
Thermal → Chemical → Mechanical → Electrical energy
Chemical → Mechanical → Electrical → Thermal energy
Nuclear → Thermal → Mechanical → Electrical energy

questions.explanation: A is correct. Coal combustion releases chemical energy as heat (thermal energy), which converts water to steam driving a turbine (mechanical energy), and the generator converts rotation to electricity. Option D describes a nuclear power plant, which uses fission, not combustion. Option C is wrong because electrical energy cannot precede mechanical in this chain. Option B inverts the chemical and thermal stages — coal does not start as thermal energy.

questions.stem: A simple pendulum swings freely without air resistance. At its mean position (lowest point of the swing), which statement about its mechanical energy is correct?

options.option_text: Total mechanical energy becomes zero at the mean position
Kinetic energy is maximum and potential energy is minimum
Kinetic energy equals potential energy exactly at mean position
Potential energy is maximum and kinetic energy is minimum

questions.explanation: B is correct. At the lowest point the bob moves fastest (maximum speed → maximum KE) and sits at the lowest height relative to the reference (minimum PE). Option D describes the extreme ends of the swing (highest points), where the bob momentarily stops. Option C (KE = PE) holds at an intermediate height, not at the lowest point. Total mechanical energy remains constant throughout — it is never zero as long as the pendulum swings.

questions.stem: A body of mass 5 kg initially at rest is acted upon by a constant net force of 20 N on a frictionless surface for 4 seconds. What is its kinetic energy at the end of 4 seconds?

options.option_text: 320 J, computed using KE = force × velocity at that instant
640 J, applying work-energy theorem: W = ΔKE = ½mv²
1280 J, computed as mass × acceleration × total distance only
160 J, using average velocity (v/2) instead of final velocity

questions.explanation: B is correct. From F = ma: a = 20/5 = 4 m/s². After 4 s, v = u + at = 0 + 4×4 = 16 m/s. KE = ½mv² = ½×5×256 = 640 J. Option C (1280 J) drops the ½ factor — the most common slip. Option A (320 J) confuses instantaneous power (F×v = 20×16 = 320 W) with energy. Option D (160 J) incorrectly substitutes average velocity (8 m/s) into the KE formula instead of final velocity.

questions.stem: A stone of mass 2 kg is released from rest at a height of 30 m. At what height above the ground does its kinetic energy exactly equal its potential energy? (Take g = 10 m/s²)

options.option_text: 10 m above the ground (one-third of the total drop height)
20 m above the ground (two-thirds of the total drop height)
15 m above the ground (exactly half the total drop height)
12 m above the ground (two-fifths of the total drop height)

questions.explanation: C is correct. Total ME = mgh = 2×10×30 = 600 J. At height x: PE = 20x and KE = 600 − 20x. Setting KE = PE: 600 − 20x = 20x → x = 15 m. The KE = PE crossover always occurs at h/2 for free fall from rest. Option A (10 m) satisfies KE = 2PE, not KE = PE. Option B (20 m) satisfies PE = 2KE. Option D (12 m) has no physical basis in this problem.

questions.stem: A spring with spring constant 500 N/m is compressed by 0.2 m and then released. What is the elastic potential energy stored in the compressed spring?

options.option_text: 50 J, calculated using full expression kx² omitting the ½ factor
5 J, obtained by applying ½kx without squaring the compression
10 J, correctly using the formula ½kx² = ½×500×0.04
20 J, derived using kx alone without the ½ factor or squaring

questions.explanation: C is correct. PE = ½kx² = ½ × 500 × (0.2)² = ½ × 500 × 0.04 = 10 J. Option A (50 J) omits the ½ — the most frequent exam error. Option B (5 J) forgets to square x (uses 0.2 instead of 0.04). Option D (20 J) uses neither ½ nor squaring. The ½ arises because the spring force increases linearly from 0 to kx, making the average restoring force kx/2, not kx.

questions.stem: An electric motor with 80% efficiency lifts 200 kg of water to a height of 15 m in exactly 1 minute. What is the electrical power consumed by the motor? (Take g = 10 m/s²)

options.option_text: 500 W, equal to the useful output power, ignoring efficiency loss
400 W, obtained by multiplying output power by the efficiency ratio
625 W, input power = output power ÷ efficiency = 500 ÷ 0.8
750 W, computed by mistaking motor efficiency as 2/3 instead of 4/5

questions.explanation: C is correct. Useful output power = mgh/t = 200×10×15/60 = 500 W. Since efficiency η = output/input, input power = output ÷ η = 500 ÷ 0.8 = 625 W. Option A (500 W) ignores efficiency — the motor must consume more than it delivers. Option B (400 W) multiplies instead of dividing (500×0.8), a classic sign-flip error. Option D (750 W) arises from misreading 80% as 66.7%. Rule: electrical input power always exceeds useful mechanical output power.

questions.stem: A spring (k = 1000 N/m, compressed 0.1 m) launches a 0.5 kg ball horizontally from the edge of a table 5 m high. Ignoring friction and air resistance, what is the total mechanical energy of the ball immediately after launch? (g = 10 m/s²)

options.option_text: 5 J, counting only the kinetic energy received from the spring
25 J, counting only the gravitational potential energy at table height
30 J, summing KE gained from spring and gravitational PE at height
55 J, adding spring PE and gravitational PE as two separate stores

questions.explanation: C is correct. Spring PE converts entirely to ball's KE: ½kx² = ½×1000×(0.1)² = 5 J. Gravitational PE of ball at height 5 m: mgh = 0.5×10×5 = 25 J. Total ME = KE + gravitational PE = 5 + 25 = 30 J. Option A (5 J) neglects the gravitational PE the ball already possesses while sitting on the table. Option B (25 J) ignores the kinetic energy added by the spring. Option D (55 J) double-counts by adding the spring's stored energy (5 J) on top of the gravitational PE, but the spring PE has already transformed into the ball's KE — it cannot be added again as a separate 5 J.
